comparison: Both evaluations support the statistical findings on maternal behavior effects on vocal practice duration (C7-C10, C41-C49, C109, C122). OpenEval emphasizes the statistical rigor and appropriate controls, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'The behavioral analyses are convincing' and praise the distinction between display number vs. display rate. Peer review R1 also includes syllable characteristics claims (C60-C69) not in OpenEval R1.

Both evaluations support findings on maternal behavior effects on learned syllable characteristics (C60-C69). OpenEval R2 focuses specifically on these syllable analyses with detailed statistical validation, while peer review R1 groups these with practice duration findings, noting that 'Statistical models identify female display behavior as a predictor of... (iii) song composition and (iv) syllable maturation.'

Both evaluations support the correlation between maternal activity and acoustic change in B2 syllables (C100, C101). OpenEval notes the appropriate use of Spearman correlation and acknowledges the correlational nature, while peer reviewers accept the finding and praise 'The authors' additions have significantly improved the clarity of their acoustic terminology and syllable analyses.'

Both evaluations address the null findings and marginal trend regarding repertoire size (C50-C52, C107-C110). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (N=10) and speculative interpretation, while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting both significant and null results as part of convincing behavioral analyses.

Both evaluations support the study design and methodological approach (C37, C136-C141). OpenEval notes the appropriateness of ad libitum sampling and acknowledges the indirect measure limitation, while peer reviewers explicitly praise the methodology as 'convincing, using longitudinal acoustic recordings and behavioral monitoring' and describe the dataset as 'impressive.'

Both evaluations support the observational findings about pup-initiated interactions (C38-C40, C117-C118). OpenEval notes the 80% figure and reasonable inference about maternal feedback, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings through their overall positive evaluation of behavioral analyses.

Both evaluations support findings on sex differences in vocal development (C81-C84). OpenEval notes this as a confirmed observation notable given songbird patterns, while peer reviewers explicitly state 'Added discussion of pup sex differences provides useful context and intriguing speculation about the role of female pup babbling.'

Both evaluations support background claims about S. bilineata vocal learning (C4-C6, C20-C26, C53-C57). OpenEval emphasizes support from multiple citations to prior work, while peer reviewers accept these as established context, describing the species as 'one of the few mammals known to exhibit vocal production learning.'

Both evaluations support the distinction between babbling and begging and observations about female behavioral displays (C28-C36, with overlap on C32-C34). OpenEval provides detailed reasoning about structural and contextual differences, while peer reviewers acknowledge 'The authors qualitatively describe specific patterns of female displays during pup babbling.'

Partial overlap on syllable characteristics (C61, C63, C66, C69). OpenEval R2 focuses on statistical support for maternal behavior effects on learned syllables, while peer review R2 emphasizes that outcomes 'were not influenced by the number of nearby adult males,' focusing on null findings regarding male tutor effects.

Both address the observation that adult males did not directly interact with pups (C113). OpenEval R17 treats this as a standalone observational finding consistent with social structure, while peer review R2 groups it with findings about male tutor effects not influencing outcomes.

OpenEval supports claims about territorial song structure and individual variation in pup babbling (C58-C59). No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these descriptive claims.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the speculative hypotheses about functions of babbling and song learning (C70-C80, C85-C89), noting they are reasonable but not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these functional hypotheses.

OpenEval supports the comparative vocal learning literature summary (C91-C99, C102-C103, C111-C112, C119-C121), noting appropriate citations and acknowledgment of debates. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these literature review claims.

OpenEval supports the acknowledgment of limitations and uncertainties (C104-C106, C114-C116), praising appropriate scientific caution. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these limitation statements.

OpenEval supports background context claims (C1-C3, C11-C17, C123), noting they are well-established and appropriately cited, though C123 could benefit from more specific support. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims.

OpenEval supports species characteristics descriptions (C124-C135, C139) as appropriately documented with references. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these species background claims.
OpenEval supports the observation of individual variation in maternal behavior (C45) as a straightforward finding. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this claim.
